content: Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More EN RegisterLog In Ask AI Search AI Mode Medscape Medical NewsFeatures Florida Tallies Highest Locally Acquired Dengue Cases in 100 Years Alicia Ault October 23, 2026 0 1 Add to Email Alerts Jump to Key Points As the number of locally acquired dengue cases in Florida has risen to levels not seen in almost a century, the CDC held a call for clinicians to inform them on how to spot signs of the mosquito-borne illness and how to treat infected individuals. Dengue, known as “breakbone fever” because of the severity of aches and pains associated with infection, is spread through the bite of mosquitoes — primarily the daytime-feeding Aedes aegypti — infected with the virus. The illness is common in tropical and subtropical areas worldwide, and incidence has skyrocketed over the past two decades, fueled in part by climate change, according to the World Health Organization. On the call, CDC officials said that as of October 15, Florida had reported 368 locally acquired cases in eight counties. “This is the largest locally acquired dengue outbreak in Florida since the 1930s,” said Laura Adams, DVM, MPH, epidemiologist with the Dengue Branch at the CDC’s National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases. There are four dengue virus types; most Florida infections have been with dengue virus serotype 2, said Adams. Cases have been reported in all age groups, but most have been in adults aged 30-49 years. Half are in men. SUGGESTED FOR YOU About 47% of those infected required hospitalization, said Adams. The Florida Department of Health is reporting an even greater number of cases. As of October 17, the state had tallied 425 locally acquired dengue cases in 11 counties. The greatest number — 346 — have been in Hillsborough County, which encompasses Tampa. Pinellas County, which includes St. Petersburg, has reported 51 cases. By comparison, Florida had reported 650 locally acquired cases from 2010 to 2025, according to historic CDC data. Hillsborough, Pinellas, and Pasco counties have repeatedly extended dengue-related states of emergency to shift funds into aerial spraying to kill mosquito larvae. Until this year, cases had also been rising in Texas, California, Arizona, and Hawaii, but none of those states have reported any locally acquired illness in 2026. Virginia, however, reported its first locally acquired case earlier in the year, said Adams. Six US territories and freely associated states also have frequent or continuous dengue transmission: Puerto Rico, American Samoa, the US Virgin Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands, and the Republic of Palau. Older adults and those with comorbidities such as asthma, diabetes, obesity, and hypertension are at higher risk for dengue. Pregnancy has been associated with a higher risk for progression to severe disease, Adams said, adding that a second dengue infection also increases severity risk, but not a third or fourth infection. Abrupt-Onset Fever and Rash About 3-14 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito, the 20%-40% of people who become symptomatic will have an abrupt fever, nausea and vomiting, mucosal bleeding, cough and sore throat, rash, and marked flushing of the face, neck, and chest. Patients might also develop a macular or maculopapular rash that starts on the trunk and spreads across the face and limbs, said Liliana Sánchez-González, MD, MPH, CTropMed, of the CDC’s National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases, on the call. Most patients seek care during this febrile phase, which can last 2-7 days, she said. They are also viremic during this phase. If the fever abates, most patients improve. Some might present with or develop more severe symptoms, which constitute warning signs that the patient might slip into a more critical phase. Those patients may have abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, ascites, altered mental status, and a progressive increase in hematocrit. “Any mucosal bleeding is a warning sign in dengue, and it is important to ask about bleeding that might not be obvious during the physical examination, including changes in the color of the urine or stools and changes in menstrual flow,” said Sánchez-González. About 5% of those who are infected and symptomatic develop severe dengue, which is marked by plasma leakage and can lead to shock, respiratory distress, severe bleeding, and damage to the heart, brain, and liver. Supportive Care Is the Main Treatment There is currently no approved dengue vaccine that’s available in the US, so prevention is primarily achieved through eliminating mosquito breeding areas and telling people to use insecticides and clothing to ward off bites. There are diagnostics available through state and local health departments and some private labs, said Sánchez-González. A reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction test combined with an immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibody test, or a dengue nonstructural protein 1 antigen test plus IgM, can detect dengue within 7 days of symptom onset. A negative result does not rule out infection. IgM antibodies are detectable for up to 90 days, so it is the recommended diagnostic test after a week. But, said Sánchez-González, “clinical management should not be delayed while waiting for laboratory confirmation.” The standard of care for dengue is supportive management — primarily administering intravenous fluids and strictly monitoring intake and outflow — as there is no curative. Patients with severe dengue may require emergency treatment that includes oxygen and close monitoring of hematocrit. Dengue patients should never be given corticosteroids, as there is no evidence of utility, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, as they could increase bleeding risk, said Sánchez-González. The agency also recommends against intramuscular injections or prophylactic platelet transfusions. CDC has created a dengue clinical management pocket guide that provides algorithms for outpatient and inpatient management. Alicia Ault is a Saint Petersburg, Florida-based freelance journalist whose work has appeared in many health and science publications, including Smithsonian.com. You can find her on X @aliciaault and on Bluesky @aliciaault.bsky.social. title: Mosquito Saliva Protein Fragment Boosts Dengue Virus Replication in Immune Cells
excerpt: A C-terminal fragment of the Aedes albopictus salivary protein 34k2 binds DENV-2 virions with high affinity and enhances viral replication while reshaping inflammatory signaling in immune cells.

content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 28, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Mosquito Saliva Protein Fragment Boosts Dengue Virus Replication in Immune Cells by October 28, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Mosquito Saliva Protein Fragment Boosts Dengue Virus Replication in Immune Cells Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A laboratory study has pinpointed the precise region of an Aedes albopictus salivary protein that binds dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2) and enhances its replication in immune cells. The protein, known as 34k2, was already known to promote DENV-2 infection, but the functional domain responsible had remained undefined. The new work, published in Parasites & Vectors, identifies the C-terminal portion of the protein as the viral-binding site and shows that this fragment alone is sufficient to potentiate viral replication and alter inflammatory signaling. The researchers used AlphaFold3 structural prediction and ZDOCK molecular docking to localize the interaction interfaces between 34k2 and DENV-2 virions. From these predictions they constructed two truncated variants: an N-terminal fragment designated rAlb-34k2-I and a C-terminal fragment designated rAlb-34k2-II, corresponding to residues 148 to 322 of the full protein. Surface plasmon resonance measured how tightly each fragment bound to DENV-2 particles. The binding results were decisive. The C-terminal fragment rAlb-34k2-II bound DENV-2 virions with high affinity, with a reported dissociation constant of 2.88 nanomolar, while the N-terminal fragment rAlb-34k2-I showed no measurable binding. This asymmetry indicates that the viral-binding capability of 34k2 resides specifically within its C-terminal region rather than being distributed across the protein. Functional assays followed in two human and mouse immune cell lines: RAW264.7 macrophages and THP-1 monocytes. When cells were pre-incubated with rAlb-34k2-II before viral exposure, the fragment significantly enhanced DENV-2 replication and the production of infectious plaque-forming virus, as assessed by immunofluorescence, plaque assays and quantitative RT-PCR. These are in vitro cell culture findings, so they demonstrate a mechanism in isolated cells rather than an effect measured directly in human infection. Beyond facilitating replication, the salivary fragment reshaped the inflammatory response of the immune cells. Both rAlb-34k2-II and the full-length rAlb-34k2 protein significantly upregulated the transcription of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IL-1β and the chemokines CCL2 and CXCL2 in vitro, measured by qPCR and ELISA. The response followed a distinctive kinetic pattern: a transient early spike in inflammatory cytokines was followed by sustained expression of chemokines. To extend the findings beyond cell culture, the team used a murine footpad injection model. Injection of the full-length 34k2 protein into the footpad induced a pro-inflammatory profile in the local tissue that was consistent with the in vitro results, supporting the idea that the protein’s immunomodulatory activity operates in living tissue and not only in cultured cells. The authors conclude that the C-terminal fragment of Ae. albopictus 34k2 constitutes a high-affinity viral-binding domain that potentiates DENV-2 replication and modulates host inflammation. They propose that targeting this specific salivary–viral interface could support the development of competitive decoy peptides or next-generation salivary-based vaccines aimed at interrupting arboviral transmission. Such applications remain proposals at this stage; the study did not test decoy peptides or vaccines, and the reported effects come from structural predictions, cell culture experiments and a local murine injection model rather than from efficacy trials. The work is presented as an early-access, peer-reviewed accepted article, citable with a permanent DOI and subject to further edits before the final version of record. Its mechanistic contribution is to narrow a broad observation—that mosquito saliva can facilitate arboviral infection—down to a defined 175-residue domain, and to link that binding activity to a measurable shift in cytokine and chemokine expression. If subsequent research confirms the interface in vivo and develops inhibitors against it, the finding could inform strategies against dengue, a disease transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes whose saliva proteins are increasingly studied as modulators of viral infection and host immunity. Subject of Research: Identification of the C-terminal viral-binding domain of the Aedes albopictus salivary protein 34k2 and its effects on DENV-2 replication and host inflammation. 病毒性传染病患病率不断上升,对全球公共卫生构成重大威胁。其中,登革病毒(dengue virus, DENV)是最广泛传播的虫媒病毒感染之一,每年影响近4亿人;据世界卫生组织(World Health Organization, WHO)报告,约1%病例出现严重临床表现。学术和产业界围绕DENV的分子病毒学、流行病学模式、传播途径和治疗靶点开展了广泛研究。四价CYD-TDV(Dengvaxia)疫苗的开发标志着登革热预防的重要进展。然而,新出现的证据显示当前疫苗接种策略存在若干局限性,促使研究人员日益重视抗病毒药物的发现和开发,作为有效登革热管理的替代或补充治疗选择。共发现14种主要生物活性化合物与登革热高度相关,在登革热与生物活性化合物之间获得70个共同靶点。通过KEGG(Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes)和Metascape分析进行的蛋白质-蛋白质相互作用(protein–protein interaction, PPI)和网络通路分析显示,DENV-2靶点具有较高相关性。分子对接(molecular docking)分析显示,Globulol和Ecalyptol与两个受体1oke和1tg8 f DENV-2具有较高结合亲和力,结合能分别为?8.3和?7.6。毒性和成药性(drug-likeness)分析证实这些代谢物用于药物开发的安全性。这些发现提示蓝桉(Eucalyptus globulus)精油可能具有治疗登革热的潜力。然而,仍需使用动物模型开展进一步体内(in vivo)研究以验证其治疗效力。 研究背景与意义:登革病毒(dengue virus, DENV)属黄病毒科,含DENV-1至DENV-4四个血清型,主要由埃及伊蚊(Aedes aegypti)传播。全球近五分之二人口受威胁,每年约3.9亿感染,约50万需住院、约2万死亡;自2000年登革热(dengue fever, DF)发病率显著上升并扩展至129个国家。当前尚无获批治疗药物或有效疫苗;四价CYD-TDV(Dengvaxia)疫苗虽为关键进展,但有效性有限且不良反应限制使用,因此抗病毒药物发现成为替代或补充策略。蓝桉(Eucalyptus globulus)精油含Eucalyptol等成分,已有抗病毒、抗菌、抗炎和抗氧化报道;为明确其抗登革热潜力,研究人员开展GC-MS成分表征、杀幼虫活性评价及网络药理学和分子对接分析,以筛选其生物活性成分对DENV-2受体的作用。研究结论提示Globulol和Eucalyptol等具较高结合亲和力,毒性/成药性较好,蓝桉精油可能作为抗登革热天然候选来源,但需体内动物模型验证。 欢迎下载《揭秘单细胞测序》深入了解这一改变科研方法的新技术领 取 关键技术方法(≤250字):样本来源:蓝桉叶采自巴基斯坦Rawalpindi地区,由Arid Agriculture University, Rawalpindi, Pakistan植物学系专家鉴定。研究人员采用光伏(PV)驱动水蒸气蒸馏提取精油,GC-MS(gas chromatography–mass spectrometry,气相色谱-质谱联用;PerkinElmer Clarus 500,NIST11.L库)分析成分;以埃及伊蚊IV龄幼虫进行杀幼虫生物测定(62.5–1000 ppm,Temephos阳性对照,probit分析LC50与LC90);用SwissTargetPrediction、DisGeNET、GeneCards、DAVID、STRING、KEGG和Metascape开展网络药理学与富集分析;用AutoDock Vina对DENV-2受体1TG8和1OKE进行分子对接,并以ProSA、Ramachandran和MolProbity评估模型;用Protox-III、Lipinski五规则和SwissADME评估毒性与成药性。 3.1 Larvicidal Activity of E. globulus Essential Oil Against Ades Aegypti:通过24、48、72、96和120 h暴露及62.5–1000 ppm浓度梯度,死亡率呈时间与剂量依赖:24 h为33%–73%,48 h为46%–80%,72 h为60%–80%,96 h为66.6%–86.6%,120 h为70%–90%;结论为精油对埃及伊蚊幼虫具杀灭活性。 3.2 Phytochemical Profiling of E. globulus Essential Oil:通过PV蒸汽蒸馏和GC-MS,10 kg叶得约45 mL精油,鉴定25种化合物;D-Limonene与Eucalyptol合计>80%,均属terpenoid(monoterpenoids和sesquiterpenoids),并含(?)-Globulol、Longifolene等,为后续分析提供成分基础。 3.3 Metabolite and Disease Targets:通过SwissTargetPrediction预测,代谢物靶点多与信号、免疫、炎症和外源刺激相关;D-Limonene关联核受体、Family A GPCR(G蛋白偶联受体)、CYP450(细胞色素P450)和代谢酶,Eucalyptol关联CYP450、转移酶、氧化还原酶、水解酶和裂解酶,Thymol关联电压门控离子通道、氧化还原酶和GPCR;提示多靶点潜力。 3.4 Metabolite-Disease Common Targets:通过DisGeNET和GeneCards疾病靶点与代谢物靶点交叉,获得70个共同靶点;CD38和MAPK14为关键重叠基因,涉及免疫细胞信号、细胞因子产生、钙动员、p38 MAPK应激/炎症/免疫调节及病毒复制相关过程。 3.5 Gene Ontology (GO) Analysis:通过DAVID GO(Gene Ontology,基因本体)富集,分子功能(MF)中heterocyclic compound binding的p值为9.818×10?13、chemokine ligand binding为6.436×10?3;生物学过程(BP)富集于viral processes(p=2.486×10?3)及T细胞谱系定向、T细胞稳态和白细胞介导免疫;细胞组分(CC)富集于线粒体膜和细胞器外膜,提示靶点集中于病毒过程与免疫应答。 3.6 Pathway Enrichment Analysis:通过KEGG(Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes)和Metascape通路富集,共同靶点富集于VEGF(血管内皮生长因子)信号、sphingolipid信号、IL-17(白细胞介素-17)信号、T细胞信号和platelet activation;37%靶点与登革热高度相关,提示应激信号与免疫激活相关。 3.7 Molecular Docking Analysis:通过AutoDock Vina对接1OKE(DENV-2包膜蛋白结构域III)和1TG8(NS3(非结构蛋白3)丝氨酸蛋白酶),正文称Globulol和Eucalyptol对1OKE具较高结合亲和力(Globulol ?8.3 kcal/mol、Eucalyptol ?7.6 kcal/mol),Eucalyptol对1TG8为?7.6 kcal/mol、Limonene为?6.8 kcal/mol;原文正文与表格对个别配体—受体对应数值存在差异,解读时保留原文数值;结论提示这些成分可能干扰病毒附着/融合或NS3蛋白酶活性。 3.8 Toxicity Prediction and Lipinski Rule of Five:通过Protox-III和Lipinski五规则,Eucalyptol与Globulol对肝毒性、神经毒性、心脏毒性和致癌性均预测为inactive;Thymol和Longifolene对神经毒性部分active,Limonene对心脏毒性轻度active;LD50最高为Longifolene 5000 mg/kg,其次Limonene 4400 mg/kg、Eucalyptol 2480 mg/kg;所选代谢物均无Lipinski规则violation,提示安全性和成药性。 3.9 Swiss ADME Analysis:通过SwissADME(absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion,吸收、分布、代谢、排泄)分析,所有代谢物位于colored zone,提示口服生物利用度适宜。 讨论部分总结:原文指出药用植物是药物发现的重要来源,网络药理学整合系统生物学、生物信息学和药理学,可从“一药一靶”转向“多成分—多靶点—多通路”。登革热尚无特异抗病毒治疗,Dengvaxia有效性和不良反应受限;蓝桉长期用作驱蚊,Eucalyptol等为重要成分。原文认为杀幼虫的时间/剂量依赖毒性与Eucalyptol、Limonene、Globulol等可能靶向GABA(γ-氨基丁酸)受体或章鱼胺能受体有关;70个共同靶点、GO中response to chemical和heterocyclic compound binding富集、Metascape登革热相关富集及分子对接结果共同支持其抗DENV-2潜力。 研究结论翻译:登革病毒感染全球负担日益加重,凸显对有效抗病毒药物的迫切需求。本研究通过综合的计算机模拟(in silico)分析,从蓝桉精油中鉴定出14种与登革热具有潜在治疗相关性的主要生物活性化合物。网络药理学和通路富集分析显示其与DENV-2靶点显著相关。分子对接表明Globulol和Eucalyptol对关键病毒蛋白(1OKE和1TG8)具有较强结合亲和力,提示潜在抑制活性。毒性和成药性评估证实这些代谢物的安全性,支持其进一步药物开发候选资格。总体而言,这些发现突出蓝桉精油作为抗登革热天然来源的潜力,值得通过适当动物模型进一步体内验证。 India Advertisement Why Kadayanallur pilot is crucial for India’s dengue vaccine rollout Public health expert Dr Chandrakant Lahariya explains Qdenga’s efficacy, safety concerns, India’s indigenous dengue vaccine candidate and why surveillance and mosquito control remain essential Lavanya Prabhakaran 23 Oct 2026 12:32 PM Click the Play button to hear this message in audio format Dengue remains a major public health challenge in India, with gaps in diagnosis and reporting making the actual disease burden difficult to estimate. With Takeda’s Qdenga vaccine receiving regulatory approval in India and an implementation pilot planned in Tamil Nadu’s Kadayanallur, in Tenkasi district, questions remain about its safety, effectiveness and suitability for wider public vaccination. Advertisement × PLAYSTREAM 00:00 StayNext 00:00 Ad will close in:click to close Speaking to The Federal, public health specialist and vaccines expert Dr Chandrakant Lahariya discusses the evidence behind Qdenga, the lessons from earlier dengue vaccines, the progress of India’s indigenous vaccine candidate Dengyol, and how the Kadayanallur initiative could help prepare the country for a broader rollout. Edited excerpts: Where does dengue stand in India today in terms of cases, deaths and geographical spread? Is India's current dengue surveillance strong enough to measure the impact of a vaccine? Nearly two decades ago, it was largely associated with major cities and metropolitan areas, but today dengue is spreading into rural areas. The disease surveillance, including dengue surveillance, remains suboptimal in the country despite National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC)’s official figures. Also read: Dengue: TN records 15,796 cases this year, highest in India Official figures recorded around three lakh dengue cases and 500 deaths in 2023. In 2024, the reported numbers were approximately 2.5 lakh to 3 lakh cases and around 300 deaths. By September this year, approximately 1.2 lakh cases and 130 deaths had been reported. These figures do not reflect the actual disease burden, but they provide an indication of its scale, as underdiagnosis and underreporting remain significant challenges. India has been working to improve disease surveillance through initiatives such as the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme and laboratory networks. However, many people seek treatment in the private sector, where reporting remains relatively poor. Surveillance in rural areas is also inadequate. The introduction of a dengue vaccine presents a valuable opportunity for India to strengthen its dengue surveillance system. How important is the Kadayanallur pilot programme and what results is it expected to generate? India's drug regulator, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), has granted marketing authorisation for Qdenga, the dengue vaccine developed by Takeda. The vaccine can now be considered for introduction in the country, subject to the relevant implementation decisions. However, before a vaccine is introduced more widely, it is important to understand the practical challenges involved in delivering it on the ground. Such initiatives help assess operational feasibility, identify challenges and understand public responses to vaccination. They also provide an opportunity to identify communication gaps and determine the training requirements of healthcare workers. The clinical trials required before regulatory approval would already have been conducted globally. Qdenga has received regulatory approval in more than 35 countries, and India's regulator has also approved it. The immediate requirement is to understand how the vaccine can be delivered effectively through the public health system. Advertisement The initiative should also provide early indications of adverse events and how effectively they are managed. Also read: Kerala reports 3 more communicable disease deaths; Shigella cases at 59 The findings from Kadayanallur could offer useful guidance when Tamil Nadu and other Indian states consider introducing the dengue vaccine. What does the available evidence say about Qdenga's safety and effectiveness? Which concerns are legitimate, and how does the vaccine work against the different dengue serotypes? Qdenga, also known as TAK-003, is a live-attenuated, tetravalent dengue vaccine. This means it contains weakened dengue viruses designed to stimulate an immune response without causing the disease in the way a natural infection would. The vaccine targets all four dengue virus serotypes: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4. Following clinical trials, the recommended schedule consists of two subcutaneous injections administered three months apart. In July, India's CDSCO approved Qdenga for individuals aged four to 60 years. However, regulatory approval does not automatically mean that a vaccine should be included in the national immunisation programme. The decision to introduce it into a public health programme requires a separate assessment of operational feasibility and public health priorities. The Phase III clinical trials of Qdenga were conducted across countries in Asia and Latin America, enrolling approximately 20,000 children and adolescents. The vaccine demonstrated an efficacy of 80.2 per cent against laboratory-confirmed symptomatic dengue. It also reduced hospitalisation by approximately 90 per cent among vaccinated participants compared with those who were not vaccinated. Follow-up data extending to four and a half years after the second dose showed that the vaccine retained an efficacy of 61.2 per cent against symptomatic dengue and 84 per cent against dengue-related hospitalisation. These results indicate that Qdenga can provide meaningful protection against dengue. However, its safety profile must continue to be monitored, particularly as vaccination expands to larger populations. What are the possible side effects of Qdenga? So far, Qdenga has shown a favourable safety profile. However, some minor adverse events can occur, including pain at the injection site, headaches, muscle aches, fatigue and temporary fever. One rare but serious adverse event is anaphylaxis, a potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that requires immediate medical attention. Also read: Bharat Biotech, Gavi-UNICEF deal to cut malaria vaccine price by 40 pc Brazil's post-marketing surveillance found that approximately 1.4 million doses of Qdenga had been administered, with 43 reported cases of anaphylaxis. This translates to around 3.3 cases per 100,000 doses. None of those reported cases was fatal. This experience indicates that, with effective emergency response systems and adequate preparedness, such reactions can be managed. Although anaphylaxis is potentially life-threatening, timely recognition and appropriate treatment are essential. Another concern with dengue vaccines is the possibility of vaccine-associated enhanced dengue. This refers to the potential for a subsequent natural dengue infection to become more severe in some vaccinated individuals. This concern emerged with earlier dengue vaccines, and it remains important to monitor for such outcomes with Qdenga. What lessons should India draw from countries such as Brazil, where Qdenga has already been introduced? When India plans a dengue vaccination programme, it can draw on lessons from previous immunisation initiatives, while also learning from the experiences of Brazil and other countries where Qdenga is being used. The process should be guided by experts and public health specialists to ensure that implementation decisions are based on evidence. It is important to consider not only the vaccine's clinical efficacy but also the practical requirements of delivering it to eligible populations, maintaining the cold chain, training healthcare workers and communicating effectively with the public. These considerations will determine how successfully the vaccine can be integrated into India's existing public health infrastructure. How is Qdenga different from Dengvaxia and what should India watch for? Dengvaxia was not licensed in India, although it was approved in other countries. It demonstrated efficacy against all four dengue serotypes, but a major safety concern emerged involving what is known as antibody-dependent enhancement. One key difference between the two vaccines is their underlying viral backbone. Dengvaxia was developed using a yellow fever virus backbone, whereas Qdenga uses a dengue virus serotype 2 backbone. Also read: France reports first human case of livestock virus Shamonda, patient dies Qdenga has demonstrated protection against symptomatic dengue in clinical trial populations that included both people who had previously been infected with dengue and those who had not. So far, the antibody-dependent enhancement concern associated with Dengvaxia has not been established with Qdenga. As Qdenga is introduced into new populations, Indian health authorities must maintain strong surveillance to identify any unexpected safety signals, including severe dengue following vaccination and subsequent natural infection. How close is India’s indigenous vaccine DengiAll to roll out? India is making encouraging progress with its indigenous dengue vaccine candidate, DengiAll, being developed by Panacea Biotec in collaboration with the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR). The vaccine is undergoing Phase III clinical trials. Like Qdenga, DengiAll is a live-attenuated, tetravalent dengue vaccine. It uses dengue virus strains originally licensed from the US National Institutes of Health. One potentially important difference is the dosing schedule. Qdenga requires two doses administered three months apart, whereas DengiAll is being developed as a single-dose vaccine. If the single-dose vaccine proves safe and effective, it could offer considerable logistical advantages. Panacea Biotec announced in January 2026 that enrolment had been completed. Participants are to be followed for two years after receiving the vaccine or placebo to evaluate efficacy, safety and immunogenicity. An indigenous vaccine could potentially improve the availability of doses and offer advantages in affordability. denguedengue vaccinedengue symptomspublic health expert About the AuthorLavanya Prabhakaran Lavanya Prabhakaran is Assistant Editor with The Federal. content_title: Human Dengue Study Reveals How Preexisting Immunity Shapes Secondary Infections
content: Dengue [BlackJack3D / iStock / Getty Images Plus] Roughly half of the world’s population is now at risk of dengue, with an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring each year. The viral infection (also known as break-bone fever) is more common in tropical and subtropical areas of the world. Currently, prevention relies on control of the mosquito vector that transmits the virus. Dengue virus has a particularly unique challenges, and is especially pernicious compared with many other viruses, as secondary infections can be worse than the first. Now, a new Phase I trial involving controlled infections in human volunteers provides new details about how preexisting immunity and anti-dengue antibodies affect the nature of secondary infections with dengue. The work is published in Science Translational Medicine in the paper, “Dengue virus controlled human challenge reveals that preexisting immunity shapes viral replication and broadly protective responses.” The findings are among the first to glean insights using a large controlled human challenge, and could inform future therapeutics and the design of more broadly protective vaccines. Secondary infections with dengue are often the most severe ones because preexisting antibodies can boost viral counts and raise the risk of severe symptoms. This has frustrated the development of badly needed vaccines for dengue. Furthermore, it’s been challenging to understand how pre-infection affects dengue outcomes, as animal models have many limitations and patients usually don’t present until after viral counts have peaked. In this study, researchers recruited 45 healthy adults who had either zero, one, or more than one prior infection with any of the four strains of dengue virus (DENV1-DENV4). The volunteers received injections of a live, weakened strain of DENV3 in a challenge study, allowing the researchers to fully interrogate dengue immunity dynamics in humans in a safe and controlled setting. The findings led to various conclusions: for example, people whose antibodies boosted the replication of the virus had the highest viral counts and waning of CD8-bearing T cells and antibodies. Additionally, people who had higher amounts of antibodies against the viral nonstructural protein 1 displayed more balanced immune responses and lower viral counts. More specifically, the authors write, “Viremia was associated with more, but still mild, clinical signs and symptoms, and secondary infection resulted in greater viremia, neutralizing antibodies, and protective T cell responses. However, those whose baseline antibodies most efficiently increased dengue virus replication in an in vitro assay experienced delayed inflammatory and adaptive immune activation, the highest viremia, strong acute immune responses, and waning of potent CD8+ T cells and antibodies. In contrast, higher baseline antibodies against the nonstructural protein 1 of multiple serotypes predicted early interferon and balanced immune activation, viremia control, and development of enduring, potent B and T cells, revealing how vaccines can induce broad, long-­lasting protection.” “Collectively, this work confirms multiple hypotheses generated by natural history studies and reveals the optimal conditions for inducing potent and persistent immunity against DENV1 to DENV4,” they note. Open sidebar AD US News CDC Issues Emergency Response Over Dengue Surge in Florida The step comes after a jump in cases in Florida and the Republic of Marshall Islands. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print An Aedes aegypti mosquito on human skin in a lab of the International Training and Medical Research Training Center in Cali, Colombia, on Jan. 25, 2016. Luis Robayo/AFP/Getty Images Zachary Stieber Senior Reporter 10/28/2026|Updated: 10/28/2026 0:00 X 1 The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has launched an emergency response to the surge in Florida of cases of dengue, a disease caused by a mosquito-borne virus, the agency confirmed on Oct. 28. “CDC is working with public health leadership to support the dengue outbreak response,” Laura Adams, commander in the U.S. Public Health Service and an epidemiologist with the CDC’s Dengue Branch, told The Epoch Times via email. The activation of the level 3 emergency response was done to provide additional support to Florida and the Republic of the Marshall Islands, which are dealing with dengue outbreaks, “as well as to prepare for possible increased transmission in other areas of the United States,” Adams said. The activation means the CDC is deploying its own staff, including personnel from the CDC’s Emergency Operations Center, to affected areas, and enables the coordination of activities such as epidemiologic investigations and laboratory testing. The CDC is deploying entomologists, epidemiologists, and laboratory experts to Florida to help with trapping mosquitoes, investigating cases, and optimizing lab equipment, Adams said. The CDC has sent personnel to the Marshall Islands to help with the outbreak response, including training local workers and providing rapid tests. Dengue is a disease caused by dengue viruses, which are spread to people through mosquito bites. Symptoms can include aches and pains, nausea, and rash. The disease is fatal in a small percentage of cases. Related Stories Florida Reports Dozens More Cases of Mosquito-Borne Dengue Virus CDC Deputy Director Departing Just Months After Appointment There is one vaccine for the disease available in the United States, and it is only recommended for children aged 9 to 16 who have previously had dengue and are living in areas where dengue is common. The best method of prevention is avoiding mosquito bites, according to the CDC, and treatment involves resting, staying hydrated, and taking acetaminophen to control fever and reduce pain. Florida has recorded a surge in dengue cases this year. In its last update, the Florida Department of Health said 425 cases have been locally acquired, primarily in Tampa and the remainder of Hillsborough County. One person, an 80-year-old woman, has died of the disease, officials told local outlets. Another 320 cases associated with travel have been recorded in 2026 in the state. Hillsborough County, Pinellas County, and Pasco County have declared emergencies over the outbreak. They have directed residents to cut down on places mosquitoes congregate, including standing water in tarps and birdbaths; to wear long clothing outside; and to apply insect repellent when leaving the home. The number of cases in Florida is much higher than has been logged in recent years, Adams told clinicians during a recent call. She said that most cases have been caused by dengue virus type 2, and that about half have required hospitalization. Overall, four U.S. jurisdictions, including Puerto Rico, have reported 1,819 locally acquired cases in 2026, according to a CDC database. The Republic of the Marshall Islands, a sovereign nation that the United States assists with defense and other support, has reported hundreds of cases in recent weeks. The president of the nation, comprising islands in the Pacific Ocean southwest of Hawaii, recently declared a state of disaster over the dengue outbreak and the impacts of El Nino conditions. The declaration said that the outbreak “is placing additional demands on government health services, personnel, supplies, and other resources.” We had a problem loading this article. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 28, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Mosquito Saliva Protein Fragment Boosts Dengue Virus Replication in Immune Cells by October 28, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Mosquito Saliva Protein Fragment Boosts Dengue Virus Replication in Immune Cells Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A laboratory study has pinpointed the precise region of an Aedes albopictus salivary protein that binds dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2) and enhances its replication in immune cells. The protein, known as 34k2, was already known to promote DENV-2 infection, but the functional domain responsible had remained undefined. The new work, published in Parasites & Vectors, identifies the C-terminal portion of the protein as the viral-binding site and shows that this fragment alone is sufficient to potentiate viral replication and alter inflammatory signaling. The researchers used AlphaFold3 structural prediction and ZDOCK molecular docking to localize the interaction interfaces between 34k2 and DENV-2 virions. From these predictions they constructed two truncated variants: an N-terminal fragment designated rAlb-34k2-I and a C-terminal fragment designated rAlb-34k2-II, corresponding to residues 148 to 322 of the full protein. Surface plasmon resonance measured how tightly each fragment bound to DENV-2 particles. The binding results were decisive. The C-terminal fragment rAlb-34k2-II bound DENV-2 virions with high affinity, with a reported dissociation constant of 2.88 nanomolar, while the N-terminal fragment rAlb-34k2-I showed no measurable binding. This asymmetry indicates that the viral-binding capability of 34k2 resides specifically within its C-terminal region rather than being distributed across the protein. Discover more Biology textbook sales Study Biology Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Functional assays followed in two human and mouse immune cell lines: RAW264.7 macrophages and THP-1 monocytes. When cells were pre-incubated with rAlb-34k2-II before viral exposure, the fragment significantly enhanced DENV-2 replication and the production of infectious plaque-forming virus, as assessed by immunofluorescence, plaque assays and quantitative RT-PCR. These are in vitro cell culture findings, so they demonstrate a mechanism in isolated cells rather than an effect measured directly in human infection. Beyond facilitating replication, the salivary fragment reshaped the inflammatory response of the immune cells. Both rAlb-34k2-II and the full-length rAlb-34k2 protein significantly upregulated the transcription of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IL-1β and the chemokines CCL2 and CXCL2 in vitro, measured by qPCR and ELISA. The response followed a distinctive kinetic pattern: a transient early spike in inflammatory cytokines was followed by sustained expression of chemokines. To extend the findings beyond cell culture, the team used a murine footpad injection model. Injection of the full-length 34k2 protein into the footpad induced a pro-inflammatory profile in the local tissue that was consistent with the in vitro results, supporting the idea that the protein’s immunomodulatory activity operates in living tissue and not only in cultured cells. The authors conclude that the C-terminal fragment of Ae. albopictus 34k2 constitutes a high-affinity viral-binding domain that potentiates DENV-2 replication and modulates host inflammation. They propose that targeting this specific salivary–viral interface could support the development of competitive decoy peptides or next-generation salivary-based vaccines aimed at interrupting arboviral transmission. Such applications remain proposals at this stage; the study did not test decoy peptides or vaccines, and the reported effects come from structural predictions, cell culture experiments and a local murine injection model rather than from efficacy trials. Discover more Genetic testing kits Get Health Tips Health health chemical The work is presented as an early-access, peer-reviewed accepted article, citable with a permanent DOI and subject to further edits before the final version of record. Its mechanistic contribution is to narrow a broad observation—that mosquito saliva can facilitate arboviral infection—down to a defined 175-residue domain, and to link that binding activity to a measurable shift in cytokine and chemokine expression. If subsequent research confirms the interface in vivo and develops inhibitors against it, the finding could inform strategies against dengue, a disease transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes whose saliva proteins are increasingly studied as modulators of viral infection and host immunity. Subject of Research: Identification of the C-terminal viral-binding domain of the Aedes albopictus salivary protein 34k2 and its effects on DENV-2 replication and host inflammation. Request Free Sample Speak to Analyst Dengue outbreaks are accelerating investment in vaccine research, Wolbachia-based mosquito control, advanced diagnostics and surveillance technologies as governments strengthen disease prevention and healthcare preparedness worldwide. Rising dengue infections are accelerating global investment in vaccine research, innovative mosquito-control technologies and integrated disease-prevention strategies. Bangladesh is considering dengue vaccine clinical trials amid a severe 2026 outbreak, while India approved its first dengu vaccine in July 2026. Advances in Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes, biological control and disease surveillance are creating opportunities for pharmaceutical companies, biotechnology researchers and public-health organisations. Dengue is an increasingly significant global healthcare challenge, driven by climate change, urbanisation, population movement and inadequate mosquito-control infrastructure. The World Health Organization (WHO) reported approximately 14.6 million dengue cases and more than 12,000 related deaths in 2024, marking the largest recorded annual outbreak at that time. Recent developments highlight a shift beyond conventional fogging and insecticide spraying towards vaccination, clinical research, improved diagnostics and sustainable vector control. Bangladesh’s consideration of vaccine trials and India’s regulatory approval of Qdenga underscore the growing importance of preventive healthcare investment. However, prevention remains challenging because of four dengue virus serotypes, variations in vaccine performance, affordability constraints and the need for sustained community participation. Consequently, emerging opportunities extend beyond vaccine manufacturers to biotechnology firms, diagnostic developers, mosquito-control technology providers, research institutions and healthcare infrastructure operators, supporting a broader, integrated approach to dengue prevention and control. Why Is Dengue Increasing Global Demand for Preventive Healthcare? Dengue transmission is increasing pressure on healthcare systems, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. Spread primarily by infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, the disease thrives in areas with stagnant water and inadequate sanitation. The World Health Organization reported approximately 14.4 million dengue cases and 11,201 deaths globally in 2024, with Brazil and India among the affected countries. Rising infections are encouraging governments to strengthen early diagnosis, disease surveillance and preventive healthcare investments. In Bangladesh, increasing hospitalisations and deaths in 2026 have intensified consideration of dengue vaccine clinical trials. Severe dengue requires hospitalisation and supportive care, increasing healthcare expenditure and demand for medical infrastructure. Opportunities are emerging in vaccine research, diagnostic testing, mosquito-control technologies and digital surveillance. However, commercial growth depends on regulatory approval, affordability, clinical evidence and effectiveness in high-transmission settings. Unlock exclusive market insights. Blog news—Download the Brochure now and dive deeper into the future of the Market How Is Vaccine Research Changing Dengue Prevention? Dengue vaccine research is transforming prevention strategies by combining immunisation, clinical evaluation and public-health surveillance. The virus has four serotypes: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4. Infection with one serotype does not guarantee protection against others, making balanced immune responses and long-term safety monitoring essential. In July 2026, India approved Takeda’s Qdenga (TAK-003), its first approved dengue vaccine, for individuals aged 4–60 years. The vaccine targets all four serotypes and uses a two-dose schedule, with doses administered three months apart. Commercial availability is anticipated in 2027, subject to applicable requirements. Takeda’s partnership with Biological E could support manufacturing expansion, while Indian Immunologicals is developing another vaccine candidate. Internationally, the World Health Organization prequalified Qdenga in May 2024, recommending its use for children aged 6-16 years in high-transmission settings. Meanwhile, Bangladesh is considering clinical trials amid its 2026 outbreak, potentially generating locally relevant safety and efficacy evidence. Key challenges include serotype-specific protection, adverse-event monitoring, immunity duration, affordability, cold-chain logistics and equitable distribution. Vaccination must complement mosquito control, diagnostic surveillance and timely clinical care for effective, sustainable dengue prevention. Why Are Wolbachia and Other Mosquito-Control Technologies Gaining Attention? Conventional dengue prevention relies on eliminating stagnant water, applying larvicides, spraying insecticides and educating communities. However, insecticide resistance, hidden breeding sites and inconsistent community participation can limit effectiveness, encouraging investment in innovative biological-control technologies. One promising approach uses Wolbachia, a naturally occurring bacterium introduced into Aedes aegypti mosquitoes to reduce their ability to transmit dengue viruses. Unlike conventional insecticides, this method aims to establish mosquito populations with reduced transmission potential. A cluster-randomised controlled trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, demonstrated a 77% reduction in virologically confirmed dengue incidence and an 86% reduction in dengue hospitalisations in Wolbachia-treated areas compared with untreated areas. These findings highlight its potential, although effectiveness can vary across locations. In August 2025, the Pan American Health Organization and international partners conducted training on sterile-mosquito and Wolbachia-based technologies involving participants from 18 countries across the Americas. Other innovations include sterile-insect techniques, geographic information systems, predictive weather models and digital surveillance platforms. These technologies create opportunities for biotechnology companies, mosquito-rearing facilities, monitoring equipment providers and specialised service operators. However, successful implementation requires regulatory oversight, environmental assessment, community engagement and sustained monitoring alongside conventional mosquito control. Market Statistics Global Dengue Cases: Approximately 4.6 million suspected and confirmed dengue cases were reported across the Americas in 2025. Global Dengue Deaths: Dengue continued to cause substantial global mortality in 2025, although a consolidated annual worldwide death total requires verification. India Dengue Cases: India reported 232,425 dengue cases in 2024, while the final 2025 total requires confirmation from national surveillance data. Bangladesh Dengue Outbreak: Bangladesh experienced a significant dengue outbreak in 2025, increasing demand for hospitalisation, diagnostics and mosquito-control services. Dengue Vaccine Development: WHO-prequalified Qdenga remained an important vaccine-prevention development in 2025 following its prequalification in May 2024. Wolbachia Effectiveness: A clinical trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, demonstrated a 77% reduction in dengue incidence and an 86% reduction in dengue hospitalisations. International Vector-Control Training: In August 2025, PAHO and international partners conducted training on Wolbachia-based and sterile-mosquito technologies involving participants from 18 countries across the Americas. What Challenges Could Slow Dengue Vaccine and Mosquito-Control Adoption? Despite technological advances, dengue prevention faces scientific, operational and financial challenges. The virus has four serotypes, DENV-1 to DENV-4, requiring vaccines to demonstrate adequate protection across different strains, sustained immunity and acceptable safety profiles. Regulatory approval does not guarantee immediate availability, affordability or inclusion in national immunisation programmes. Safety monitoring remains essential. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, October 28, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology Older Donors’ Immune Cells Show Distinct Galectin Response to Dengue Virus in Lab Study by October 26, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Older Donors' Immune Cells Show Distinct Galectin Response to Dengue Virus in Lab Study Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Older adults with dengue face higher risks of adverse outcomes, but the contribution of age-related immune responses remains uncertain. A laboratory study published in Virology Journal compared how immune cells from older and middle-aged donors respond when exposed to dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2) in culture. The researchers found that cells from older donors released higher amounts of two soluble proteins, galectin-3 and galectin-9, at later time points, while concentrations of most other measured mediators were generally lower. The study used peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) drawn from volunteer donors: ten older donors aged 65 years or above, with a median age of 74.9 years and an observed range of 65.8 to 92.0 years, and ten middle-aged donors, with a median age of 39.4 years and an observed range of 34.8 to 49.1 years. In the laboratory, the PBMCs were exposed to the DENV-2 strain TH-36 at a multiplicity of infection of 5. To track the immune response over time, the team collected culture supernatants before exposure and at 24, 48, and 72 hours after DENV-2 exposure. They then measured nine soluble mediators: GM-CSF, IFN-γ, IL-6, IL-10, MCP-1, TNF-α, and VEGF-A, along with galectin-3 and galectin-9. Discover more Check Symptoms Study Biology Order DNA Kits Donate to Research Study Chemistry The most pronounced differences emerged late in the culture period. Compared with cultures from middle-aged donors, cultures from older donors had higher galectin-3 concentrations at both 48 and 72 hours. At 48 hours, the median galectin-3 concentration was 363.6 pg/mL in older donor cultures versus 197.8 pg/mL in middle-aged donor cultures, with an exploratory p value of 0.0412. By 72 hours, the gap widened: 810.1 pg/mL versus 218.5 pg/mL, with a p value of 0.0011. Galectin-9 followed a similar late pattern. At 72 hours, older donor cultures showed a median concentration of 219.6 pg/mL compared with 92.23 pg/mL in middle-aged donor cultures, a difference that reached a nominal p value of 0.0355. The reported differences in galectin-9 were concentrated at this late time point. In contrast to the galectins, the seven other measured mediators were generally lower in older donor cultures across the 24 to 72 hour window. The authors also noted that IFN-γ, IL-10, and TNF-α differed between the groups even at baseline, before any virus was introduced, indicating that some differences in circulating immune mediator levels were already present in the donors’ blood. The authors frame these findings as exploratory. The between-group p values at each time point were unadjusted comparisons, and interpretation of the nominal significance levels is limited by the small sample size of ten donors per group and by the multiple comparisons performed across nine mediators and four time points. The study also did not test statistical associations between cytokine and galectin concentrations, so the relationship between the two patterns remains an open question. Discover more Get Health Tips Read Med Journals Study Anatomy Compare Lab Gear Biology textbook sales There are further limits on what the results can tell us. The experiments used an ex vivo culture model, in which isolated PBMCs are exposed to virus in a dish rather than within the full complexity of a living immune system. This design cannot establish causal mechanisms or clinical outcomes, and the findings may not translate directly to how older patients respond to dengue infection in the body. Despite these caveats, the study makes a methodological point: the authors conclude that the contrasting pattern highlights the value of examining galectins alongside other soluble mediators when investigating variation in responses to DENV-2. A measurement strategy limited to the standard cytokine panel would not have captured the elevated galectin concentrations observed in the older donor cultures. According to the authors, the small sample and the culture model limit causal and clinical inference, and larger donor-linked experiments and studies in patients with dengue are needed to assess the reproducibility and clinical relevance of the findings. Until such studies are conducted, the reported differences in galectin-3, galectin-9, and the seven other mediators remain an ex vivo observation rather than an explanation of clinical outcomes in older adults with dengue. content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Destination Thanh Hoa Thanh Hoa police are stepping up measures to prevent and control dengue fever caused by the Dengue virus. Faced with the growing threat of dengue fever outbreaks caused by the Dengue virus, the Thanh Hoa Provincial Police are proactively implementing a comprehensive set of measures to prevent and control the epidemic; strengthening public awareness campaigns, monitoring health and environmental hygiene, promptly controlling risk factors, limiting the spread of the disease, and protecting the health of officers, soldiers, and the people. Công an tỉnh Thanh Hóa•24/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 According to statistics from October 16, 2026 to the present, Hac Thanh ward has recorded 7 cases of dengue fever with local transmission. Notably, in the outbreak area of ​​Doi Cung 2 residential group, 4 cases have appeared with signs of secondary transmission. Although epidemiological investigation, containment, and outbreak control measures have been urgently implemented, the monitoring results of the Thanh Hoa Provincial Center for Disease Control on the morning of October 23 still recorded mosquito breeding grounds and disease-transmitting mosquitoes in this area. In light of the above situation, the Director of the Provincial Police Department requested that police units and localities strengthen information and communication about the epidemic situation and preventive measures; diversify communication methods so that officers, soldiers, and citizens can proactively protect their own health, their families, and the community. When symptoms of illness appear, they should immediately go to a medical facility for examination, consultation, and timely treatment, and not self-treat at home. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA Police units and local authorities must proactively monitor the situation of outbreaks in their areas; proactively implement measures to protect the health of officers, soldiers, detainees, and drug rehabilitation trainees under the management of the Provincial Police, especially in units with large numbers of people living and eating together. Through this, they can promptly detect suspected cases, proactively coordinate handling, and prevent disease outbreaks within the units. Provincial Police spray mosquito repellent during the epidemic. You may also like Environmental sanitation and the elimination of mosquito breeding grounds are required to be carried out regularly and seriously. Units need to dispose of items and containers that can collect water and breed mosquito larvae; maintain weekly general sanitation, clear bushes, and unclog drains in the troop deployment area. Simultaneously, implement measures to eliminate mosquitoes and disease-carrying insects. The spraying of insecticides and chemicals to kill mosquitoes and insects during the autumn and winter of 2026 must be urgently implemented as required. Regarding the Hac Thanh Ward Police, the Provincial Police Director requested close coordination with the health sector to decisively and comprehensively implement disease prevention and control measures at the outbreak site in the area. This includes focusing on implementing professional measures as guided by health authorities, strengthening public awareness campaigns to encourage people to proactively clean the environment, eliminate breeding grounds for disease-carrying mosquitoes, and thoroughly address areas at risk of mosquito breeding, contributing to controlling the outbreak and limiting the risk of community spread. Regarding medical examination and treatment, the Provincial Police Hospital needs to prepare hospital beds, sufficient quantities of medicine, intravenous fluids, and treatment equipment, ensuring the "four on-site" principle; proactively receive, admit, and treat dengue fever patients, strictly implement regulations on infection control, ensure safe patient transfers, and minimize complications and deaths. Dengue fever, caused by the Dengue virus, is an acute infectious disease transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. The disease can be severe, causing dangerous complications and even death if not detected, monitored, and treated promptly. Therefore, in addition to the involvement of relevant authorities, the proactive awareness of disease prevention among each individual plays a particularly important role. You may also like To effectively prevent and control dengue fever, each family needs to regularly check and remove items that can collect water, clean water containers, and tightly cover tanks, jars, and pots; collect waste, and maintain a clean and well-ventilated living environment. People should cooperate with health forces in environmental sanitation campaigns, eliminating mosquito larvae and pupae, and spraying chemicals to kill mosquitoes; proactively prevent mosquito bites by sleeping under mosquito nets, wearing long clothing when necessary, and using appropriate mosquito repellent methods. When there are signs of suspected dengue fever, people should immediately go to a medical facility for examination, consultation, and timely treatment; under no circumstances should they attempt self-treatment at home. In particular, if warning signs appear such as severe abdominal pain, continuous vomiting, unusual bleeding, lethargy, or extreme fatigue, the patient should be taken to a medical facility immediately for prompt treatment. Every agency, unit, and family needs to proactively implement preventive measures, avoiding complacency and negligence, contributing to preventing the spread of dengue fever caused by the Dengue virus, and protecting their own health and the health of the community. content_title: PAHO urges Caribbean to prepare for dengue, chikungunya rise
content: PAHO urges Caribbean to prepare for dengue, chikungunya rise WASHINGTON, CMC – The Pan American Health Organisation (PAHO) is urging Caribbean countries to strengthen disease surveillance and prepare health services for possible increases in dengue and chikungunya, amid renewed transmission in parts of the Americas and the anticipated intensification of the El Niño phenomenon. In an epidemiological update issued on Wednesday, PAHO reported 1.69 million suspected dengue cases across the Americas as of mid-September, including 3,413 severe cases and 571 deaths. Although the cumulative number of reported cases was 58 per cent lower than during the same period in 2025, the agency said the decline had not been consistent across the region. It said increases had been observed in recent weeks in the Andean, Central American and Caribbean sub-regions, while all four dengue virus serotypes were circulating in the Americas in 2026. PAHO also raised concerns about chikungunya, reporting increased transmission between late 2025 and 2026, including renewed circulation in countries and territories where the virus had not been detected for several years. As of mid-September, 213,919 suspected chikungunya cases had been reported across 20 countries in the region. Of these, 78,481 were confirmed, with 88 deaths recorded. The agency also pointed to transmission in new areas, outbreaks outside historically affected seasons, longer periods of transmission and increased reports of more severe clinical manifestations. PAHO is calling for countries to strengthen epidemiological, virological and entomological surveillance, expand diagnostic capacity and ensure that cases are detected early and patients receive timely care. It also recommended stronger integrated measures to control Aedes mosquitoes, which transmit both diseases. Health services should be prepared to respond to potential increases in cases at all levels of care, PAHO said, with particular attention to strengthening primary healthcare workers’ ability to recognise dengue warning signs early and prevent progression to severe illness. Hospitals should also be ready to manage patients with warning signs and severe cases, the agency added. PAHO further urged countries to improve environmental management, remove containers that collect water and encourage communities, families, local authorities and other sectors to participate actively in mosquito prevention and control. Eliminating mosquito breeding sites remains a key measure in reducing mosquito populations, the agency said. Osprey Observer SUBMISSIONS Submit News/Press Release Bloomingdale / FishHawk Edition Current Issue Online Riverview Edition Current Issue Online Valrico Edition Current Issue Online Brandon / Winthrop Edition Current Issue Online SouthShore Edition Current Issue Online Archives 2026 Osprey Observer TV Podcasts Home Brandon / Winthrop Hillsborough County Extends Emergency Over Dengue Concerns Brandon / Winthrop County News Hillsborough County Extends Emergency Over Dengue Concerns By Marie Gilmore - October 23, 2026 108 Hillsborough County continued its response to a growing number of locally acquired dengue fever cases by extending its state of local emergency through October 22 as mosquito control crews increase efforts to reduce the mosquito population responsible for spreading the disease. County Administrator Bonnie Wise signed an executive order extending the emergency under authority granted by the county’s Emergency Management Ordinance and Chapter 252 of the Florida Statutes. The original emergency declaration was issued September 24 and has been extended in seven-day increments, including extensions through October 8, October 15 and October 22. A state of local emergency may remain in effect for seven days unless it is rescinded or extended. The declaration allows county officials and emergency managers to take certain actions more quickly to protect the health, safety and welfare of residents. It also provides a path for reimbursement of certain emergency-related expenses. Mosquito Management crews are increasing treatments by both air and ground after surveillance identified dengue virus activity in mosquito populations in multiple neighborhoods. The county is coordinating with the Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County on education and mosquito-control efforts in impacted areas. Hillsborough County has reported more than 200 locally acquired dengue cases during the outbreak, making up the vast majority of Florida’s reported cases. The outbreak has affected communities across the county, with cases identified in nearly 60 ZIP codes. Dengue is spread primarily by infected Aedes mosquitoes. Symptoms can include a sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle, bone or joint pain, nausea, vomiting and a rash. Most people recover within two to seven days. Residents should seek emergency medical care if warning signs of severe dengue develop, including severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, extreme fatigue or irritability or difficulty breathing. Residents throughout the county are encouraged to help reduce mosquito breeding areas by eliminating standing water around their homes, particularly following recent heavy rains. Residents can also sign up for notifications about localized aerial treatments in their neighborhoods and access information about current mosquito-control activities through the county’s online resources. Mosquito control services are funded in part through Hillsborough County property tax dollars. For more information, contact Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services at 813-635-5400

content: ___ Play Now Log InSign Up Florida News Listen Live National News Weird News Local Traffic Local Weather Get News Alerts Florida News Florida Dengue Cases Top 400 as Mosquito-Borne Virus Spreads By Rob Garguilo Oct 23, 2026 Photo: Brett_Hondow / iStock / Getty Images FLORIDA - Florida health officials are reporting additional locally acquired dengue fever infections as the mosquito-borne virus spreads into more counties across the state. The Florida Department of Health reports that locally transmitted dengue cases have surpassed 400 in 2026, with the Tampa Bay region accounting for most infections. Hillsborough County remains the center of the outbreak, while neighboring Pinellas and Pasco counties continue reporting additional cases. According to Pinellas County officials, 401 dengue cases have been confirmed across the three counties, representing a 14% increase from the previous week. Pinellas County has recorded 51 confirmed cases since August and extended its local state of emergency through October 29th. The declaration allows county officials to accelerate mosquito control operations and seek potential reimbursement for related expenses. Locally acquired infections have also been identified in Miami-Dade, Broward, Orange, Palm Beach and Polk counties. Seminole County recently confirmed its first locally transmitted case. Mosquito control agencies are expanding surveillance, conducting ground spraying and coordinating aerial treatments to reduce mosquito populations. Planned helicopter treatments in Pinellas County have been delayed because of high winds, with operations expected to begin next week if weather conditions permit. Dengue spreads through infected mosquito bites and can cause fever, headaches, muscle pain, joint pain, nausea and skin rashes. Severe infections may require hospitalization. Health officials recommend eliminating standing water, wearing protective clothing and applying EPA-registered insect repellents to prevent mosquito bites. content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế A 23-year-old man with critical dengue fever requires ECMO intervention. GĐXH - After 5 days of high fever, abdominal pain, and digestive disorders, the young man went into shock and suffered critical respiratory failure. Doctors had to deploy ECMO combined with continuous hemodialysis to support the patient's vital functions. Báo Gia đình và Xã hội•26/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 Dengue fever can become severe even in young people with no underlying health conditions. On October 26th, information from the Central Hospital for Tropical Diseases indicated that doctors there are treating 18 dengue fever patients, including one critical case requiring ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation) intervention. According to Dr. Pham Van Phuc, Deputy Director of the Intensive Care Unit at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, patient LTS (23 years old, residing in Tuyen Quang ) had no prior recorded underlying medical conditions. The patient developed a high fever and abdominal pain, and self-medicated at home, but their condition did not improve. By the third day, the patient also experienced frequent loose stools, nausea, and fatigue. A critically ill dengue fever patient is being treated at the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Photo: Provided by the hospital. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA The patient was taken to a nearby medical facility, diagnosed with dengue fever, and treated with intravenous fluids. However, the patient's condition continued to worsen, with significant fatigue, agitation, hypotension, and respiratory failure. The patient required intubation and mechanical ventilation before being transferred to the National Hospital for Tropical Diseases. Upon admission, the patient was in critical condition. Despite invasive mechanical ventilation with 100% oxygen, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) was only about 80%. Heart rate was rapid at 120-140 beats/minute, blood pressure was 80/40 mmHg despite the use of vasopressors. The patient was cyanotic, had cold extremities, and bilateral pulmonary hypoventilation. Laboratory results showed positive NS1 and IgM Dengue tests, along with abnormalities in liver, kidney, and coagulation functions. Doctors diagnosed the patient with dengue hemorrhagic shock, critical respiratory failure progressing to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and suspected gastrointestinal infection. According to Dr. Phuc, this is a particularly severe case of dengue fever in a young person with no underlying medical conditions. The shock and severe lung damage directly threaten the patient's life. You may also like Implement ECMO in combination with continuous renal replacement therapy to support life. Faced with severe respiratory failure and no improvement in blood oxygen levels despite mechanical ventilation at maximum oxygen concentration, doctors at the Intensive Care Unit decided to implement extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) to support gas exchange. In addition to ECMO, the patient was treated with mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, and continuous hemodialysis. A combination of resuscitation measures was employed to support circulation, manage metabolic disorders, balance fluids, and support renal function according to the patient's clinical condition. During treatment, patients are closely monitored for hemodynamic parameters, coagulation, and organ function to allow for timely adjustments to resuscitation measures. Following intensive resuscitation, the patient's blood oxygenation and hemodynamic status initially improved. The oxygen concentration delivered via ventilator was reduced to 21%, and blood pressure was recorded at approximately 100/70 mmHg while the patient was still receiving vasopressors. However, the patient still requires VV-ECMO support and intensive care measures. The patient has not yet been assessed as having passed the critical stage and needs continued close monitoring and treatment. Be vigilant for dengue fever during the period from day 3 to day 7. According to Dr. Phuc, dengue fever is an infectious disease caused by the dengue virus, primarily transmitted through Aedes mosquitoes. The disease can affect people of all ages, including young, healthy individuals without underlying health conditions. Most people with dengue fever recover, but some cases can become severe due to plasma leakage, leading to shock, severe bleeding, and organ damage. It's important to note that the critical phase usually occurs from the 3rd to the 7th day of the illness, especially when the patient's fever begins to subside or has just disappeared. This is when plasma leakage, blood concentration, thrombocytopenia, and shock can occur. Therefore, the absence of fever does not mean the patient is cured. You may also like Based on the above case, Dr. Phuc advises people not to be complacent when experiencing prolonged high fever, especially when warning signs appear such as severe or continuous abdominal pain, frequent vomiting, extreme fatigue, restlessness, lethargy, unusual bleeding, decreased urination, or difficulty breathing. When these symptoms appear, patients should immediately go to a medical facility for timely assessment and treatment. Those suspected of having dengue fever should not self-administer intravenous fluids at home or use aspirin, ibuprofen, and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) due to the risk of increased bleeding. Fluid replacement, fever reduction medication, and laboratory monitoring should be carried out according to the instructions of healthcare professionals. Besides early detection and treatment, people need to proactively prevent the disease by eliminating mosquito breeding grounds, covering water containers, destroying mosquito larvae, and avoiding mosquito bites. People can also learn about dengue fever vaccination according to age, indications, and professional guidance from doctors.
